Chapter 6: Healing Emotional Wounds and Rewriting Old Narratives
As you move forward on this journey, it’s natural to start looking inward—to notice those emotional wounds that often sit at the heart of codependent patterns. Maybe you’ve felt the sting of neglect, constant criticism, or just plain chaos in your past. These experiences can quietly shape the way you see yourself, and even how you connect with others.
So, where does healing begin? It starts with gentle, honest self-inquiry. Questions like, “What stories am I carrying about my worth?” or “Do I really believe I have the right to express my needs?” can open the door to understanding yourself on a deeper level.
For a lot of folks, those old stories run on autopilot. Maybe there’s a belief that love has to be earned through sacrifice, or that showing anger or sadness will lead to rejection. These narratives often start in childhood, helping us get by back then—but as adults, they can become invisible scripts that shape our choices, without us even realizing it.
Healing means shining a light on these old scripts and asking, “Is this really true for me now?”
Here’s a helpful metaphor: picture your mind as a forest with a well-worn path. Every time you repeat a thought or behavior, that path gets a little clearer, a little easier to walk. Healing is about noticing when you’re about to follow that old, familiar trail—and gently choosing to step off and start creating a new one. One that honors your feelings and your needs.
So, what practical steps can you take to start healing emotionally?
You might try journaling about past experiences and the beliefs they planted. Or, practice mindfulness—just noticing self-critical or anxious thoughts, without judging yourself. You can begin to swap out those old, limiting stories for new, affirming self-talk. Try telling yourself, “Hey, I’m allowed to have needs.”
And don’t forget to give yourself space to actually feel your emotions—grief, anger, sadness. Let them come up, and let them move through you in safe, healthy ways.
Sometimes, this work is easier with support. Opening up to a therapist or even a trusted friend, sharing your story out loud—it can help loosen that old narrative’s grip and bring in fresh perspectives.
Over time, the weight of those emotional wounds begins to lighten. You’ll find more room for self-acceptance and a gentle sense of peace.
Remember, healing isn’t about erasing your past. It’s about weaving it into who you are now, with compassion. Think of it like tending to a neglected garden—pulling out the weeds, nourishing the soil, and patiently waiting for new growth. Every act of self-compassion is a step toward rewriting your story, and truly believing in what you deserve.
